1000216.etyen:
Unadapted borrowing from Italian Enna, the modern Italian name of the Sicilian city. The name was officially restored in 1927, reviving the ancient name Latin Henna, also Haenna, from Ancient Greek Ἔννα (Énna). The Ancient Greek name is of uncertain origin, possibly Pre-Greek, Sicanian, or Sicel.
During the Middle Ages, the city was known as Castrum Hennae (“fortress of Henna”). This was adapted in Siculo-Arabic as قَصْر يَانِيّ (qaṣr yāniyy), and subsequently reinterpreted as Castrum Iohannis (“castle of John”), which gave Italian Castrogiovanni. The ancient name Enna was restored in 1927.

1000984.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Jóhannes, a Christian name borrowed into Old Norse from Late Latin Iōhannēs, a variant of Latin Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”). Doublet of Hans, Jan, Jens, Jo, Johan, John, and Jon.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Johannes, Danish Johannes, Swedish Johannes, Icelandic Jóhannes, Faroese Jóhannes, Finnish Johannes, German Johannes and Dutch Johannes (“male given name”).

1001496.etyen:
First attested in the 1800's. Exact origin uncertain. A Nordic female given name, probably either formed from huld (“friendly, gracious”), from Old Norse hollr (“faithful, loyal, gracious”), or derived from hulda (“secrecy, hiding; something hidden”). The latter is probably related to hylja (“to cover, hide”), from Proto-Germanic *huljaną (“to cover, veil”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, hide”).
The adjectival explanation ultimately goes back through Proto-Germanic *hulþaz (“inclined, favourable; gracious, loyal”) to a homonymous Proto-Indo-European root *ḱel- (“to lean

1001752.etyen:

Compare Danish Tilia, Swedish Tilia and English Tilly (“female given name”).
